I've watched so many of her interviews and such over the years, and I rewatched a lot of them within the last year or so after she had to cancel events for health reasons. Yeah, she was 80 and had health concerns, but to me, she outwardly seemed to be doing well enough to tamp down the whispers that she was at death's door, so I truly didn't think it would come to this, at least not yet.

As I left, knowing it was the last time I’d see him, he said “would you ask Dolly to pray for me?”  

The next day, as we chatted backstage prior to a brief concert at her Dollywood theater, I passed along my grandfather’s request.  Dolly immediately stopped all the chatter in the room and said “let’s all pray for our brother Edward.”  She then said a heartfelt prayer, gave me a hug and left the room to get ready to sing.  

I’ve become aware over the years of many, many acts of charity and kindness that Dolly performed - many more than have been made public.  She was very likely the most generous, well-meaning celebrity of our time.  And I can’t wait to read the full-life biography that someone is going write about her, which will go far beyond what she, herself, was willing to put on paper in her 1994 autobiography.  Only then will the public get to know just what a great soul she was.

There doesn't seem to be any reason to assume that the percentage of players with CTE iin the population of 638 players whose brains were not examined is any different than the percentage in the population whose brains were examined - which would lead one to conclude that the percentage for the entire population is much more like 90% than 25%.That's horrifying.

Of those they received 235 brains to study, 215 of which showed CTE. Why? What made those families decide to donate? The logical answer would be behavioral issues that made family members suspect of CTE. Perhaps not but this is a clear example of selection bias, that is, those studied are not representative of the population intended for research. And what of the 643 brains not donated for study. Again, why? Normal behavior prior to death, family not wanting to know, socioeconomic issues? Unanswered. The 24.5% rate is the floor. Is it possibly as high as 91% (215/235).

When I got out of college I went back and played some club football (soccer) over there in the lower divisions. Outside of heading the ball when needed you weren’t getting your skull banged on every play. It was rough but not a meat grinder. 

Parents, if you have a choice get your kids into the original football (soccer) because you only get one brain. If I had to do it over again I would never have played American football.  

I made good friends playing that game but what has stuck with me are not those friends, who are scattered to the wind or no longer with us, but my bent joints and three times broken nose, amongst other ailments. Those include years of bad headaches that come and go for no apparent reason and are a harsh reminder of my playing days. 

It’s up to families to make these decisions. American football isn’t going away regardless. It’s too ingrained to end. 

But it can help end a person too soon.

comments.body: If Abrams tanks are vulnerable to drones I suppose that the President’s limousine is similarly vulnerable? Conversely, if the limo can be protected then tanks can be protected.

comments.name: Mike Smith
comments.body: Last week the US Army disbanded its drone testing and research battalion. The US Army has 5,000 M1A1 Abrams tanks and the entire US Army doctrine remains based on the use of tanks. Ukraine is currently firing approximately 200,000 drones per months as ammunition. The entire US Army does not possess enough drones for 5 days of war in Ukraine. Once again, the US Army is fully prepared for WW2.

articles.title: What Happened to the Coveted Western Tanks Sent to Ukraine?
articles.summary: Ukraine pleaded for the expensive weapons, and ultimately got them, but drones have rendered them almost unusable.

comments.name: deepharbor
comments.body: I fear the US will not have racial acceptance and harmony in my lifetime.  We seem to be going backward at this point.  I take solace with the knowledge that in 50-60 years there won't be white people, or black people or yellow people there will be mixed people.  Only then will we be healed.

comments.name: Lisa Sams MSN, RNC
comments.body:
Thank you for this article as a reminder from history that we tend to forget what came before us.  When history is distorted and not considered important enough to read, debate and take school children on history tours we enter a slippery path into delusional beliefs about America. Understanding episodes of disgrace is as important as celebrating the good. 
 An entire generation has grown into adulthood with no living memory of 9/11. How much do we understand about  this tragedy came to be 25 years ago?

comments.name: bekah
comments.body:
Thanks for this fascinating and beautifully written piece. If history was taught in story like this instead of dry facts, students would be hungry for more instead of bored senseless. 

NYT does a bang up job with such stories, including two other truly memorable ones by Jonathan Darman and Dan Barry -- "If Only More Americans Could See This Place" and "On Blood-Soaked Ground, 'A Prayer for the Future' of a Divided Land," respectively.  

When I find my spirits flagging these are among the things that lift them. This adds to my personal hope-chest of America the beautiful. So thanks again, Mr. Cole.

comments.name: JV
comments.body:
This is an inspiring article. Our family is a big fan of Lafayette, and the revolution. I commented that our parents took us to bunker hill and other battle sites over vacations. 

I can’t stop thinking about this, we learned about history together-we were raised by the same parents in the same environment. History wasn’t just for vacations, it was often a topic of conversation that used to bore me as a child terribly. It was woven into our home, be it principles or military strategies. 

When we went trick or treating together, my brother loved tricorn hats and dressing like Paul revere. This is to say we both love our country deeply and wanted to serve the people of this nation somehow. 

How is it he supports Trump and I do not? 

What’s striking to me is he is the only person in my family who has not changed his support of Trump or the Republican Party. 

So this made me think- how do we move forward? We rarely even talk about politics now. I don’t get to see him often and I don’t want to argue when I do. NOTHING has been so divisive as Trump. 

I’ve tried to start talking about things we agree on, we agree on more than we disagree. I’ve done this with others and it has helped, with him, I try but- I wonder if maybe I’m scared of what he will say. 

Are families a microcosm of society? To an extent yes, but the masses arguing now don’t have the same love or history together. We must find a way forward. A modern Lafayette

comments.name: Grzdacz
comments.body:
"The ruined attempt to establish [self-government] in France"?
France experienced an Imperial period after its Revolution, and by 1825 it was indeed a monarchy - does it mean it had no self-government?  I think that it is equally wrong to say that Belgium, the Netherlands or Sweden in 2026 have no self-government because they are monarchies. Moreover, their monarchs have neither the will nor the power to send armed forces to the streets of their towns to shoot their citizens.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
I had no knowledge of this prior to today but I believe wholeheartedly that this could happen again, maybe in some other form--and not a war or other aggressive act.   We are a nation that believes in the ideal, even if we don't as individuals behave as such with our actions every day.  

I hope that the next leader will strive to be an example of this ideal and show us what is possible when we accept our mistakes as our history and aim higher so as to not repeat them.

comments.name: George
comments.body:
This wonderful article about Lafayette reminded me of a memorable day in the life of our family.  We were in Paris on July 4, 1978.  We saw an announcement about a ceremony at the tomb of Lafayette, so we went.  Turns out it was by invitation only.  My pied-noir uncle recognized the accent of the concierge at the cemetery and after a few pleasantries the concierge returned with invitations for us all (me, my wife, two kids and my French uncle.  We ended up a few meters from Madame Giscard d'Estaing (the president's wife) as she laid flowers at Lafayette's tomb.  A young female American soldier played taps.  It was very moving.

As a scientist ad/or tourist I have traveled extensively in Europe, Asia and South America.  Everywhere I went, I got the feeling that America and Americans were loved (and envied) (even by Paris waiters).  Today everything is different.  Our so called leader is despised almost everywhere and we get the blame for electing him TWICE.  Only the civil war years were more miserable than his 6 years in office.  We need another Lafayette to help rid of this lunatic despot.

comments.name: RP
comments.body:
Of course, the USA is far from perfect.

The question today is: Are you proud of the USA with its imperfections or not?

articles.title: Men Wept. Women Fainted. What Lafayette’s Tour of America Tells Us About Ourselves.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Lafayette returned to the United States in 1824. His tour carries key lessons for a country still fighting over how to remember its past.

comments.name: Fred Little
comments.body:
Crowds go wild for brutal sport because human delight in cruelty and the theatrical suffering of others is an inherent human tendency which we allow businesses to trigger, hype, and exploit on an almost entirely continuous basis. We tell ourselves "it's just business."

And the truth is, that is the nature of business in a capitalist system: the human response to human suffering is just another resource to exploit, the captured eyeballs just another opportunity for paid advertising.

comments.name: LPR
comments.body: I stopped watching 5 years ago.  I grew up with football, ran a fantasy football league, had a very large super bowl party every year at my house, and had a subscription to Red Zone.  Football was important to my family.  I quit cold turkey because of CTE.  I have heard all the arguments from friends and family why it is still "ok" to be a fan.  I just can't enjoy it anymore knowing that players are risking their lives on the field.  By the way, I was surprised to learn that it was easy to let it go.

comments.name: Stephen Fortson
comments.body: I played tackle football, beginning in 6th grade all the way through college. In my era, 1974-1982 concussions were called "getting your bell rung." You only left the field if you were knocked out cold, otherwise you shook it off, got ready for the next play, and hoped the symptoms of seeing double would go away before the next series. I didn't know the damage I was doing to myself, no one knew, including our doctors and sports medical staff. My saving grace was my dad was a doctor and encouraged me to not use football as a stepping stone to a career. He convinced me that football was not a good career and I should educate myself and seek out a career based on my academic training. Thankfully I listened to my dad and enjoyed a long career as a professor at a public university in Ohio. I'm retired now and feeling fortunate, I heeded my dad's warning and ended my football career, after a short stint trying out for the Toronto Argonauts where after a few days of hitting, my head felt like it been put in a washing machine. I remember walking to practice one morning and seeing a group of tennis players and telling myself, that's what I need to be doing.Turns out, that was the day I quit football, with no regrets. Today, I still enjoy watching my favorite football teams, but there's a simmering urge to find more productive things to with my time.

comments.name: TB0
comments.body:
Mr. Almond puts it well. For those of us who are fans, football played at the highest level is a remarkable game, full of speed, surprising gracefulness and agility from modern Goliaths. (And for anyone who’s worn a helmet and shoulder pads, seeing something like Beckham Jr.’s one-handed catch in 2014 is truly unbelievable.)

I suspect change will come from players - the NFLPA has a good amount of power, and no one coming into the game wants a 1:4 chance of CTE. That’s worse odds than Russian Roulette and what’s the point of millions of dollars if you’re too injured to enjoy it by your 40s, or worse, commit suicide? They will insist on modifications that, over time, will make the game both safer and less spectacular. That in turn may drive some fans away, but I suspect everyone will adapt. And there will be an uneasy balance between some greater level of safety, and the 1:6, or 1:10 chance of CTE that is inescapable with football in any form a fan today would recognize.

comments.name: memosyne
comments.body:
Yes!  high school football can be damaging to the brain.   A high school friend of mine had a younger brother;  Intelligent, capable, healthy, (gorgeous) and kind.   I noticed he wasn't on the school bus.  I asked his sister about him and she  told me  he had a concussion from football.  
Fast forward:   at our 50th reunion I asked my friend how her brother had done in life.   She said he had trouble in school,  couldn't handle college, couldn't keep a job.   But I remembered how smart and capable he was at age 15.   What a waste.
I can't watch football because I think of him.

comments.name: Jeff M
comments.body: At least one in four doesn't begin to cover it.  They tested what, 30% of the brains.  So 70% weren't tested.  You don't get a 93% positive rate on 30% if the other 70% have 0%.  There probably is some bias, but it can only be so much.  If the tested brains are twice as likely to have CTE, then the actual percent with CTE in total is around 60%.  Even if it's three times as likely, its around 45%.  So at the least, it's basically half of football players who will get CTE and it could be higher.  So explain to me why kids are allowed to play football?

comments.name: George
comments.body:
The crowds at NFL games, and in bars, dens and "man caves" throughout the land go wild for the same reason fans went wild watching the Gladiators vs. Lions in ancient Rome.

Football is ritualized gang warfare where one group of ruffians takes battle with another group of ruffians to provide "thrills and chills" to the viewers eager for a vicarious experience.

Oh, and football does wonders for the sale of pickup trucks and beer too....

articles.title: As C.T.E. Cases Soar, Why Do Football Crowds Still Go Wild?
articles.summary: A collision of American popular culture and public health is on display in the N.F.L.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body:
"preserving the truce with China may, for now, outweigh the benefits of taking more aggressive action against Iran."

And this is why the entire exercise is just more Trump bloviation and empty threats. His approach cannot work without China being involved, and the U.S. will not be interested in an all out trade war with China. If they did it would likely further worsen economic conditions globally (and in the U.S.) right around the midterms. There is no way they will do that. 

These threats will hang out there in the wind, there will be some sanctions against smaller nations that won't have a crippling impact, and China will happily keep buying Iranian oil and trading tech with them, as long as it keeps the U.S. busy and focused on Iran. Trump will end up hoping we all forgot as he moves back to another type of threat...blowing them to the stone age AGAIN or something like that.

comments.name: Critical Thinker
comments.body:
China is a manufacturing giant; the US manufactures little anymore. China has some internal debt, but the US is $40 Trillion in debt. I'm wondering if the US is authentically the #1 economy in the world since it manufactures little and is saddled with such an untenable debt? 

China has forged ahead in renewable energy and EV's, and BYD sales now surpass $1 Trillion, which I believe makes it the largest car company in the world. China isn't burdened with science deniers who risk children's health by cutting back or eliminating vaccinations, while measles just killed 2 more people in the US.  

No one  would bet against China's future economic success, and no one would bet on US future economic success. China will continue importing 80% of Iran's oil, and Trump is impotent to do anything about it.

comments.name: Leto
comments.body: There need to be much greater pushbacks against American wars, both military and economic, against other countries just because US doesn’t like them or they are rivals. That’s rogue behaviour that should not be tolerated by the international community.

comments.name: Beth
comments.body: This is why the campaign will fail. It never had a chance.

comments.name: Sean
comments.body: “For decades, the United States has exploited its central position in the global financial system to isolate adversaries like Iran and North Korea.”  Exploited?  Remember that these regimes are repressive un-American dictatorships, the very thing America was created to reject. That is our job to oppose them.

comments.name: Duncan
comments.body: The oil embargo against Japan in 1941 was a direct and major cause of the attack on Pearl Harbor. And Warren Buffett knew what he was talking about when he described tariffs as 'an act of war, to some degree'.

comments.name: Hector
comments.body: The lies, the self enrichment, the blatant corruption, the sheer incompetence, the voters are onto it but when are the established media outlets going to get behind what the rest of the world can plainly see. You have a leader who is not just damaging, but destroying your economy and your country. Innocent people the world over are suffering the consequences of one man's pettiness  fragility and likely mental decline meaning that this is no longer just America's problem. The sooner you speak out the sooner the issue can be properly and legally addressed.

comments.name: H. Clark
comments.body: Good for China! No one in the world will stand up to Trump like Canada and China. In fact, China should get involved militarily to support Iran. The U.S. would surrender in about thee minutes. China is in its meteoric ascendency; America is in deeply decline. China knows this, and is finally flexing its very significant economic muscle. Maybe it’s time to flex its military muscle against the U.S. The war with Iran is already over Trump’s and Hegseth’s heads; wait until Beijing gets involved. It will be a real comeuppance for the fascist regime of Donald Trump.

articles.title: China Pushes Back After Trump Tightens the Screws on Iran
articles.byline: Alexandra Stevenson, Aaron Krolik and Keith Bradsher
articles.summary: The Trump administration risks a clash with Beijing as it tries to cut off Iran’s economic lifelines without upending a fragile U.S.-China truce.

comments.name: Edorampo
comments.body: Thank you, Mr. Trump, for making Darline Graham the Republican candidate for U.S. Senate for the mid-term election in South Carolina.  Annie Andrews, Democratic candidate, now has a strong chance to win and turn the U.S. Senate BLUE. With a Democratic House and Senate, Mr. Trump will be impeached. For the third time. Hubris will be the cause of his downfall.

comments.name: Gina Smith
comments.body: It was South Carolina voters right to choose.  Too bad they had only the choice of choosing bad or worse.  Neither candidate is going to offer South Carolinians anything worthy of their vote.  Just more of the same.  Guess they really do like the warmed-over gruel they've been getting from the GOP.

comments.name: Bubbie
comments.body: I am not surprised that Darlene Graham won the senate seat, but I am saddened that the voters chose her.  It only shows once again how thinking does not enter into choosing a candidate.  Do they realize that this know-nothing person will be in this position of power for 6 long years?

comments.name: Tyto alba
comments.body: Rather than make potential supporters wary, her admission of knowing nothing but that she hates the same people they do, was a sure vote getter.  Even as their lives get worse, punishing the right people is all they care about.

comments.name: Zach
comments.body: Yeah, she won, but a five point gap between the two in a state like South Carolina sure doesn't seem to bode well for Trump's political power right now.

comments.name: RM
comments.body: Follow the money.  Graham’s allies, including PACs, outspent Norman and his allies 7 to 1.  Norman still came within 5 points of victory.  In good news, the $8 million spent on this runoff will not available to support Republicans in the general election.  But in bad news, those of us who live near swing districts are already seeing huge sums spent in dark money TV ads for Republicans in swing districts.  We need to make sure that Democratic swing candidates have the funds to tell voters to follow the money.

comments.name: Cynic
comments.body:
I dunno. Political novice seems like a polite term for the pliable sock puppet who won. 

But the choices weren't great. 

Sure, Ralph Norman is a long-term congressperson, but really...election-denier, vice-chair of the Freedom Caucus, poor speller (e.g. proponent of "Marshall law"), and so on and so on.

No winners here, yet the voters spoke.

comments.name: JimmySee
comments.body: Trump's candidate, the GOP poster child for DEI, ekes out a narrow victory in a GOP primary.  We hope the larger South Carolina electorate has better sense than to elect the inexperienced, unqualified, ill-prepared sister to Senator Graham's seat.  And here I thought the GOP did NOT support DEI!

articles.title: Even as Trump’s Standing Slips, He Slingshots a Political Novice to Victory
articles.summary: After facing low approval ratings and endorsement setbacks, the president made a show of force in lifting Darline Graham to the Republican nomination for Senate in South Carolina.

comments.name: MicheleP
comments.body: Nobody has mentioned that she never had any children. Did any journalists ever ask her about that? was it a choice, does anyone know?  Perhaps the poverty that she grew up in made her want to live a life full of glamour, without the drudgery that motherhood can often be?

comments.name: Georgia J
comments.body: Dolly Parton was a Christian. That sums her up.

comments.name: Shirley
comments.body: She was a national treasure. Her impact on childhood literacy was profound.  You can read about her Imagination Library here: https://imaginationlibrary.com/

comments.name: Stuart Keeler
comments.body: Thank you for the views and terrific piece!!  Seems to me that Dolly Parton has always understood something essential about self-expression: - As she once quipped, “If I hadn’t been a woman, I’d be a drag queen for sure.” There’s real wisdom tucked into this jest — a reminder that authenticity often means repainting the picture others expect of us until it finally looks like who we actually are.

comments.name: Shockacon2
comments.body: Let us always remember that Dolly Parton walked out of her mother's church and into a lifetime of doing the Lord's work. Much will always be made of her creative genius and her legacy in singing, songwriting, acting, philanthropy and business. I just hope that future explorations of her private, personal life and unparalleled professional achievements, will also delve deeply into the spiritual foundations on which they were built. She lived loving God and loving our neighbors as ourselves. Like Jesus, Dolly loved the little children of the world. Like Jesus, she fed the hungry, healed the sick, embraced the marginalized and never forgot the poor in the community from which she had come. She was a miracle worker. That big-hearted, beautiful, buxom blonde conveyed such a profound understanding of the humanity we all share and spread love and laughter so widely that her death has broken hearts and occasioned deep grief around the world. if God was indeed one of us, I suspect he walked among us for 80 years in the guise of Dolly Parton of Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. May she rest in peace.

comments.name: Jaz Montana
comments.body:
I had these Barbie dolls that wore over-the-top glam as  little girl in the 80s: Crystal Barbie, Peaches N' Cream Barbie. Blond, beautiful and impossibly perfect. 
In real life, on TV, there was Dolly Parton. She was my glitzy Barbie come to life!

comments.name: Doug
comments.body:
Years ago I visited an elegant hide store in the design district of West Hollywood.  The proprietor was affable, and took great pleasure sneaking me a preview of the velvety ocelot bikini they were fashioning for Dolly.

I left with a beautiful cow hide, and kindled imagination about what she did with that teeny-tiny spotted suit, on that exotic curvaceous body, onstage.  Self-deprecation and parody could not cover up such a tantalizing spectacle.

And what a genuine, loving soul she was.  My condolences to her family and fans.

comments.name: Diana Conrad
comments.body:
We all love Dolly Parton.  Never judged, got into politics, sang and wrote great songs, loved dressing up in her own style, which we all knew because we saw it for decades.  We loved her wit and songs and the way she dressed.  She was herself.  Her passing has pulled together people today in a way that is missing from our everyday lives, which is another way we grieve her.

We are left in the mire of nastiness in this country.  We lost some joy today, and it reminds us of past happier times, that there are good people in the world and how little joy we have during our daily struggles with corruption, lying, poverty and mass incompetence at our top levels of government. RIP Dolly, we will always love you.

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s Bedazzled, Bewigged and Bodacious Style
articles.summary: A wild mountain rose, she used her clothes and her body to subvert expectations.

comments.name: MScott
comments.body: I’m not sure what readers were expected to take from this, but I remain unconvinced. It was all marketing speak, from start to finish, and not one sentence about this new organization’s specific policy goals and funding.

comments.name: smartalek
comments.body:
Yet another in the unending parade of conservatives who are happy to take the goodies liberal Democrats have gotten them or given them -- Social Security survivor payments (Paul Ryan); affirmative action ("Justice" Clarence Thomas, the World's Greatest Oxymoron); federal family support (that Boebert creature, among so many others); and in Manchin's case, his entire career in the gummint he's worked so hard to diminish and disempower -- and then pull that ladder up behind them.
Further deponent sayeth not.

comments.name: Science Teacher
comments.body: No thanks, Joe.  All the "help" you gave while a supposedly Democratic senator puts us in the mess we have today.

comments.name: Eva Marie
comments.body:
A reminder that Joe Manchin's daughter engaged in drug profiteering by raising the price of the critical, life-saving Epipen by 600 percent. It appears that being an Idependent in her and her dad's view means being price gougers. Her personal fortunes rose by the millions.

I will keep both feet solidly on the Democratic side of the aisle, thank you very much.

comments.name: JW
comments.body: 43% of the electorate are now Independents. That's certainly enough to form a new centerist party guided by common sense that, in fact, represents the beliefs of a vast majority of voters. Independents, myself included, are done with the radical luncay that has been dragging the Democratic Party farther and farther to the left -- particularly the DSA (they need a trip to Cuba to have their eyes openned). The GOP is equally pathetic kowtowing to a pathological narcissistic grifter. C'mon USA, time to form a new 3rd party and get voters who want to think seriously about the issues and not simply be led by demogogues spewing simplisic, misguided ideology.

comments.name: Rick Spanier
comments.body: Great message from the wrong messenger.  Yes, having three more independents in the senate and another 25 in the house would be a needed step to countering the dysfunctional congress and its de facto duopoly.   We need more Sanders and Kings onboard and fewer Manchins  His hypocrisy is astounding.

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: Joe Manchin is a corrupt coal money man. It is farcical that is a sensible mister plain sense man. Joe Manchin is not a good thing.

comments.name: FMJ
comments.body: Ranked choice voting is what is needed.

articles.title: Joe Manchin Pushes for More Independents to Join Congress
articles.summary: The former Democratic-turned-independent senator and his daughter are backing independent bids for the House and the Senate to try to weaken the two-party grip on the Capitol.

comments.name: Hamish
comments.body: I was very displeased to hear of her passing.

comments.name: trish otto
comments.body:
You know, every once in a while, talking with friends and family and you’re asked if you could have lunch with any living human, who would you choose?  Dolly Parton, my choice for the past twenty years.  Why?  Because she is KIND, TALENTED, FUNNY, GENEROUS and she embraced her humble beginnings.
May we all honor her by being kind to each other.

comments.name: Blanche White
comments.body:
Mr. Abumrad,

I can completely understand how you are unable to relate to how Ms Parton was able to mine her past to endlessly communicate its hardships and charm in such a way that captured people's hearts because that was the  world of our ancestors, full of similar values and drive, who came and settled all over this country and endured and strived with tremendous courage and often in terrible poverty. 

It was raw but there was also a simplicity and innocence as they lived and worked and worried together and endured and shrugged off their hardships with music forged from it.

That is the memory of so many of us, still in touch with our past and how we came to be, that Dolly Parton will always speak to in rhyme and rhythm.

We came from Europe mostly and forged a nation and though that appears harsh now and some want to criticize, that was the way of the world then. Yet nothing can be said to deny the bravery and hope of our ancestors who looked forward into the unknown and left all they knew to face a wilderness and often lost their lives to the challenge.

Some, off in the Smokies sang off their troubles and the hunger pains in their stomachs.

Those are the feelings Dolly Parton captured dressed in tinsel and unapologetically letting her roots shine!

comments.name: Esther
comments.body:
Jad, you were among the first people I thought of upon hearing the news. I listened to your podcast during Covid lockdown and it completely tuned me into Dolly Parton, an artist I was only moderately aware of, and - as a child born in the '70s - largely as a punchline.

Not only was yours one of the first podcasts I listened to, but it remains one of the best. Thank you for changing my life, and possibly Dolly's too, by introducing the real Dolly Parton.

comments.name: Sue
comments.body:
Two largely unrelated thoughts, 

(1) During his undergraduate days, my tea-totaling, hippie father-in-law was part of a small grass co-op, so later, when my kids were teens, he thought himself cool to regale them with stories of his escapades. It was lost on him that the weed of his youth shares little in common with today’s product, so perhaps it wasn’t helpful for him to romanticize his rampant drug use to my impressionable kids!

(2) The aforementioned concern aside, in the past, I actually thought it was somewhat silly to think of weed as a gateway drug and figured it was preferable for them to get high than to drink. But then I realized, teens have to buy weed from drug dealers, and who wants their kid to have A DEALER? The weed, even today’s mega powerful strains, isn’t the gateway, it’s the access to other drugs via a dealer that’s especially problematic 

Either that or the bad influence of Grandpa Gabs-a-lot, who knows.

comments.name: Amy
comments.body: Jad, thank you so much for the wonderful podcast. I listened to it twice and will probably listen again! You brought out her mystery and depth and multi- dimensionality. We all love her because she loved us. But you kept it from being sappy. What a magnificent force for good she was.

comments.name: Laura M.
comments.body: Very comforting to read this tonight--thank you for writing this so quickly. We need these words about our country's secular saint. I will listen to your podcast again, which moved me so much when it was released, and recommend it to anyone who will listen.

comments.name: Jane Reader
comments.body: That's one of my favorite podcasts, and I was hoping you'd write something about her. Incredible person and your ability to capture her essence is also special. Thank you, Jad.

articles.title: What Dolly Told Me
articles.summary: Trailing Dolly Parton around the world, I witnessed so many small moments in which she’d gracefully own her power without the slightest hint of fight.

comments.name: CharlesRVA
comments.body: When people wonder why housing is so expensive, this would be why.

comments.name: Laurence
comments.body: Well done, gentlemen.

comments.name: Jd
comments.body:
The houses are stunning. I'm heading to Red Hook this weekend and will pass by to see them in person because I like architecture, especially this style.

Marvels of architecture and engineering they may be and heck a tree was saved! What's not to like except the price tag, but quality costs. 

To weave this story as a win for a nature and the love of a tree? So romantic. Sounds like a fairy tale to me, or sales pitch.

Four rowhouses totally around 30-40,000 sq ft from what I read, replaced one 2,250 sq ft 1899 house in a sorry state on a very large, ramshackle, overgrown lot. This means that almost every square inch of the plot is now covered in structure, leaving an 18 sq ft driveway and 8 sq feet at the back of each house.

A tree was saved but the open space of the yard and garden were sacrificed in the name of square footage. A roof terrace, lovely as that is, doesn't equally replace what was lost.

Yeah, I know, I'm really fun at parties.

The real environmental win, if there is one, is the porous driveway, which will not only help water the tree but hopefully lessen run-off of rainwater in a neighborhood prone to flooding (and is of benefit to the houses as well).

If it were my 400K, I would have used that money to build houses with smaller footprints, bigger yards and a tree or maybe two in each yard, but I'm a dreamer, and a tree lover.

comments.name: Heide Fasnacht
comments.body: Anyone who strives to save a mature tree is very high on my list. It is most unfortunate that the boondogle flood abatement project in Lower Manhattan involved felling well over mature 500 trees. Could they not have been saved?

comments.name: Kat
comments.body: So many haters when it comes to silver maple trees. Two years ago I purchased an old house in an old neighborhood where all my neighbors had sanitized their yards with small non-native trees, hostas and lots of lawn. I have a large silver maple tree in my south-facing front yard which provides day-long dappled shade and a home to a variety of birds. It’s beautiful and I love it! And despite some very strong storms, it has done no damage so far. I hear through the grapevine that the neighbors become very unhappy about the leaves blowing into their yards in the fall. They don’t realize my tree is providing their yard with much needed sustenance!

comments.name: Flyover Country
comments.body:
Applaud the effort, but it's barely sticking your finger in the dike to hold back the flood.  Only when the public thru their elected officials demand less density and the related less lot coverage allowance is there any hope to avoid the coming stormwater crisis.

Rather than bleat the whataboutism, I'll say that for my part at least, it's difficult to sense the moment that a movement crosses a line until you're a little way beyond it. I wouldn't say I utterly disavow every idea from that time as frivolous or "intentionally provocative;" I believed a lot of that stuff because it seemed like a continuation of my values and the quest for equality and fair treatment.

I think what I've learned is not that the ideas were wrong, but that it was too far, at the wrong time, in the wrong way, by the wrong people. I was along for the ride while we were trying to make the world a better place. When the purity tests seemed to require self hatred and the cancelation of good people who were my friends, I snapped out of it a bit.

It isn't wrong to want police to treat people fairly. It isn't even wrong to say that they haven't demonstrated the responsibility to manage themselves. But is "defund" a good political or even policy move? Heck no.

It's a bit like a mathematician refusing to come out for drinks because Zeno's paradox says that he'll never actually get there, failing to realize that there's such a thing as close enough.

comments.name: Matt Cook

Alexander Von Humboldt was the first anckno environmental scientist. Von Humboldt was exploring South America in 1800. “After he saw the devastating environmental effects of colonial plantations at Lake Valencia in Venezuela in 1800, Humboldt became the first scientist to talk about harmful human-induced climate change… He warned that humans were meddling with the climate and that this could have an unforeseeable impact on ‘future generations.’” (P.5, “The invention of Nature: The Adventures of Alexander Von Humboldt The Lost Hero of Science.”)
Also from page 5 of Andrea Wulf’s excellent biography: “Charles Darwin wrote that ‘nothing ever stimulated my zeal so much as reading Humboldt’s Personal Narrative’ saying that he would not have boarded the Beagle, nor conceived of ‘The Origin of Species’ without Humboldt.” 

What directly followed Von Humboldt was the development of environmental science. The 1864 book, “Man and Nature,” by George Perkins Marsh is a deep and well documented work on all aspects of environmental research. Much significant work on environmentalism closely followed and constantly appeared in scientific research and public knowledge, up to this day.

There may be reasons why we have destroyed our own planet, but there is no excuse for our refusal to respond to the documented and demonstrated evidence of more than two centuries.
The “unforeseeable impact on future generations,” Humboldt warned about turns out to have been truly foreseen, long ago.

The current contours of the game are creating a very avoidable health catastrophe. Recent rule changes protecting players from play likely to produce brain injuries must be expanded and above all strictly enforced. There should be no more close calls when it comes to dangerous play. If a player acts in a way that triggers a "close call scenario" he should be removed from that game. And penalties for dangerous play must be successively even more stringent, so that players who insist on endangering their fellow players are tagged and eventually removed from the sport altogether. Football can change to become a safer sport, but new rules for increased player safety must be instituted .... and then strictly enforced.

comments.name: Robert Rosenthal

As I understand the current study the only brains that were examined were volunteered for the study upon the death of the former NFL players. From a scientific perspective there are issues with the sample. Considering that the players most likely exhibited symptoms prior to their death - which is why their brains were volunteered -there is a high probability that the sample is primarily made up of individuals who are likely to have CTE.   That would mean that the results are skewed and can't be statistically extrapolated to all NFL football players. From a statistical perspective it is also not  comparable to younger football players.
That being said, the study does demonstrate that there is a risk of CTE from playing professional football (although not to the degree claimed in most media reports). There is also a risk from collision sports to children as there are risks to children from riding bycycles on streets and other physical and sport activities, as well as from teenage driving. Gun violence kills many children in the United States. Parents (with input from their children) should weigh all risks when making their decisions.

- First, as some comment already mentioned, attackers need only succeed once. Defenders need 100% success, all the time.
- Second, it seems like some people expect AI to magically find all the vulnerabilities, and make our application secured once and for all. But there is and will be no such thing as perfect code. Therefore, defendants will always have to upgrade systems, which is incredibly costly. On the attackers side, all you have to do is retry with the next llm as soon as it gets released.

My thoughts about pieces like this on education are simple: the record of academic (i.e. from unuversity eductaion departments) are so awful in the medium or long run that I discount anything like "studies" of or by their programs.  

I taught college for 43 years at a departmkent ranked #6 in the country. I found that the abilities of the students never changed over that period. About 50% had abysmal abilities, about 3% were brilliant, the others spread equally in between. The racial makeup did change (Asian up, everybody else down with their relative makeup unchanged). But interestingly I noticed one clear difference: over the years the number of students in the middle third  coming in for help, and those in the top 3% coming in to ask questions (usually "why"), not for help, rose a lot. That didn't happen for merely "good" or "bad" students. 

None of the methodologial changes they had experienced seem to have changed their abilities. I still therefore think that abilities are determined at conception, in the DNA. But this was a very technical subject.

A version of her discussion of Demosthenes seems to be in the New Republic in 2013. There she argued that due to Demosthenes' phillipics against Philip of Macedon (yes that seems to be where the expression originates), Athens eventually became enslaved and lost their freedom, when they could have cut a better deal. Yet, Pericles made a similar claim when he urged Athenians to hang onto their own empire against the Spartans decades earlier in the Peloponnesian War. The causes of that earlier war and the fact that the Athenians did not follow Pericles' advice and he died of the plague before he could have any further influence on them, don't detract from the fact that nobody thought he was wrong to urge Athenians to remain free. And in America, we also didn't want to be part of another empire just as Athenians did not want to be Macedonians. It may be true that Athenians suffered under bad demogogues. But, Antipater who she mentioned in the New Republic article, was the executor of Aristotle's estate, a great philosopher, but not exactly a friend of democracy either. Now 83, I feel that The NY Times has left me behind in its trek towards a new form of liberalism that reverses the liberalism I grew up with.

Emily Wilson describes the translation of the two classics by Homer thus:

"Wilson says that translation is a “fraught” process inevitably filled with “compromise.” Every choice entails a departure from the original."

Which raises the question:  Why have languages disappeared from the education of most Americans who pretend to be educated.

Not that my own understanding of languages is all that sharp.  I did study Latin in high school for two years and read parts of Caesar's Gallic Wars at a glacial pace.

But I gathered something from the experience.  The terseness of the rhetoric spoke volumes.  Only gradually did I become aware that Caesar had committed genocide in his conquest of Gaul.

Homer's Iliad provides similar insight into how war was regarded by the ancients.  The war stopped so that BOTH SIDES could mourn the death of the Trojan hero Hector.  That spoke volumes.

My own conclusion is that the ancients felt forced into war by Malthusian forces.  They understood what contemporary liberals have forgotten:  The wages of two many children is wars forced upon society.  But the ancients tried to make sense of a process that caused one man to kill another.

Liberals fails to come to grips with the fact that resources on planet earth are running out due to population growth.

The war in Iran is a harbinger of a dark future.

comments.body:
The dynamic of canonical literature is less about universal human discovery and more about the ongoing machinery of cultural self-legitimation. When a dominant global language endlessly recycles its foundational texts, it creates a feedback loop that mistakes imperial reach for philosophical primacy.
Translating texts like the Odyssey into contemporary vernacular certainly exposes the raw mechanics of an ancient epic. Yet, it also highlights how immense institutional time and resources remain locked in a narrow orbit. The endless refurbishing of European classical antiquity reinforces the illusion that these texts are the primary bedrock of human thought. In the process, rich African historical traditions are reduced to mere regional folklore, while deep, continuous Indian and Chinese philosophical systems remain unread and fundamentally misunderstood.
More critically, this over-indexing relies on a form of generational narcissism. It frames current human progress as the linear outcome of a specific ancient lineage, mistaking self-admiration for historical reality while ignoring how little these specific texts actually account for the complex drivers of modern existence. Spending so much cultural capital repeatedly re-exhuming a single fraction of human history erases the broader global web of thought that truly shaped where we stand today.

“My husband and I want to start a family soon, but I dread telling my in-laws…. How can I set boundaries or tell them politely to keep their thoughts about my pregnancy to themselves?”

Most competent therapists will tell you that you can’t change other people’s behavior. You can only manage your own behavior and how you will react to others. 

The whole concept of boundaries is often misunderstood. A “boundary” isn’t a rule of behavior you impose on other people. It’s a decision you make about how YOU will behave certain situations. 

For example, “If this person starts shouting, I will hang up the phone.” Or “If my partner drives us to dinner and decides to drink alcohol, I will call a cab to go home.” 

You can “share your boundaries” with others, and they might change their own behavior, but don’t count on it. You can only count on your decision to follow through. 

In this case you can say “I’m well informed about this pregnancy and I don’t want to discuss it further. Let’s talk about your up-coming trip.” And then you change the subject. 

You can’t control their behavior. Only your own. 

That said, *every prospective grandparent on earth* is going to want to discuss the pregnancy with the mother of their future grandkids. Another way to look at this is that at least they are educated in the subject and not just sharing “heath factoids” they saw on social media. 

Sometimes your current situation *feels better* when you realize how much *worse* things could be.

Phoenicians, Greeks, and Romans were the foundational pillars that wove and formed Western civilization. Byblos was the main seat of the Phoenicians as they expanded their influence across the Mediterranean, reaching as far as the British Isles to trade for tin and exploring the Atlantic coast of Africa. They were the first civilization to build truly seaworthy boats, and the Phoenician alphabet serves as the basis for our modern script. Remarkably, they managed to spread a far-reaching culture and influence through trade rather than war and conquest. They were also perhaps the earliest society to practice a form of democracy in selecting their leaders, who functioned more like CEOs of a trading enterprise than hereditary dynastic kings. 

I sincerely hope the international community can apply the necessary pressure to prevent further destruction to that historic land.

In Vulgar and Medieval Latin, the phrase ‘ab oculis’ literally means ‘without eyes’ which evolved to ‘enveigle’ with the meaning shifting from physical blindness to blinding someone's judgment using clever tricks or charm.

Because it shares its deepest roots with the Latin word for eye (oculus) it’s related to the words ocular, inoculate, optics, myopia (nearsightedness), and autopsy (literally ‘seeing for oneself’).
